title: Karna's abandonment
hook: a charioteer and his wife find a basket on the river, and raise the boy inside as their own
carry: let go upstream, taken in downstream

segments.voice: Yesterday, Karna's abandonment happened: a shining baby in a basket, and a frightened mother blessing him from the bank — a person on each side of it. Did you look for the fear behind someone's hard choice? Day seven hundred thirty.

Downstream, a man and his wife are by the water. He's Adhiratha, a charioteer, a suta, someone whose work is driving and caring for the chariots of warriors. She's Radha. The text tells us they have no child. And floating toward them comes a basket. They pull it to the bank, open it, and find a baby boy, glowing, in armor and earrings. Yesterday we stood with the mother who let go. Today the story crosses the river and stands with the parents who catch.
screen: `DOWNSTREAM: ADHIRATHA AND RADHA.` → `A BASKET ON THE WATER.` → `A BOY INSIDE.`

segments.voice: Adhiratha and Radha take the boy home and raise him as their son. There's no hesitation in the telling, no long debate. They wanted a child, and here is one. They give him a name: Vasusena. The name points back at what he was found wearing, the armor and earrings he was born with. Later the world will know him as Karna. He's also called Radheya, son of Radha, after the woman who raised him, not the one who bore him. Hold onto that name. Now here's what the river has done. Karna was born to a princess and a god. He's grown up in the house of a charioteer. In the world of the Mahabharata, that matters. Birth decides a great deal: who may compete, who may rule, who gets laughed at. For most of his life Karna will carry royal blood he doesn't know about, and a charioteer's home he will not disown. Both will be pressed on him by others, and both will be part of who he is. And one more thing to notice. Abandonment is only half of this story. The other half is adoption. A child let go upstream is taken in downstream. Karna will carry both halves all his life: the loss from upstream, and the home from downstream.
screen: `TAKEN IN AS THEIR OWN.` · `VASUSENA, AND KARNA.` · `RADHEYA: SON OF RADHA.` · `A PRINCE'S BLOOD, A CHARIOTEER'S HOME.` · then, large: `LET GO UPSTREAM, TAKEN IN DOWNSTREAM.`

segments.voice: Settle, and give the breath room. Someone once took you in when they didn't have to. A teacher, a neighbor, a friend's family, a stepparent, a coworker in your first week. Picture their face for a moment. Remember one specific kindness, the smallest one you can find: a meal, a lift, a word at the right moment. Let it sit in the chest, without needing words. The bell holds the time.
Karna's abandonment. A basket caught downstream, a charioteer and his wife, and a boy named Vasusena, Radheya, Karna.
Your line: let go upstream, taken in downstream. Today, thank one person who took you in, even in a small way. Day seven hundred thirty.

howItsDone: In retellings, Karna is also called Radheya, son of Radha, honoring the mother who raised him; listeners meet him under that name as well as Karna.

original.note: Sanskrit rādheya: son of Radha, one of Karna's names, after the mother who raised him.

trapdoor: what you thought: an abandoned child, alone.
what it means: a child let go upstream and taken in downstream by a charioteer and his wife.
what a scholar hears: the name Radheya keeps the adoptive mother in his name, and his charioteer upbringing will shape how others treat him.

notes: All paraphrase. Confirm that the text says Adhiratha and Radha were childless when they found him.
The name Vasusena is linked to the armor and earrings he was born with; no etymology of 'vasu' is stated. Confirm the text gives this link.
Radheya glossed as 'son of Radha'; confirm.
The claim that birth decides who may compete and rule is the script's framing of later scenes (the tournament); confirm it is fair.
howItsDone: 'often called Radheya' is a general claim about retellings; a Keeper may soften further.

Editor pass: cut 'says a lot about how the poem sees him' and 'a name he's proud of' (unsupported); replaced a third straight 'some readers' framing with a concrete close; practice opener varied, the 'if you pray' line (also on 726-727) removed, and the listener is no longer told what to feel.

Audit pass (2026-10-01): 'spend his life with royal blood he doesn't know about' corrected to 'for most of his life' (he learns his birth from Krishna and Kunti before the war); 'both will be used against him' softened, since his royal birth is later used to woo him, not to shame him.
